title: VenusX: Unlocking Fine-Grained Functional Understanding of Proteins
one_liner: VenusX is a benchmark that tests whether protein-learning models understand the detailed jobs of individual amino acid building blocks, not just the whole protein.
lead: Proteins are like factories with many parts, and each part has its own job. Current benchmarks test whether models can predict the overall job of a protein, but they ignore what each tiny piece does. VenusX is the first benchmark that asks: does your model really understand the fine details inside a protein?

problem.h2: Models see the whole protein, but miss the detailed pieces
paras: Imagine a car engine test that only checks if the car moves forward, but ignores whether the spark plugs, valves, and pistons work. That is what protein benchmarks do today. They test if a model can predict what a whole protein does, but they do not check if the model understands what each amino acid (the building block) does inside the protein.

A beginner would say: my model predicts protein function well, so it must understand how proteins work. But that is like saying a calculator that gives correct answers must understand why the math is true. The model might be pattern-matching surface signals instead of really grasping the internal structure.

callout.html: Existing benchmarks only test whole-protein predictions; they never check whether models understand which exact amino acids handle the binding, which ones are conserved over evolutionary time, or which ones are the active sites where the chemical reaction happens.

steps.text: Gather 878 thousand labels from three databases, each marking which amino acids do what.

Active sites (where chemistry happens), binding sites (where other molecules attach), conserved (unchanged over evolution), motifs (repeated patterns), domains (functional chunks), epitopes (antibody targets).
Separate proteins by evolutionary distance using three similarity thresholds: same family, distant family, unknown family.
Run protein language models, sequence-plus-structure hybrids, pure structure methods, and alignment-based techniques.
Show accuracy drops for each model type, revealing which gaps exist and which tasks are hardest.

paras: The paper introduces a new thing to measure: can models predict the fine-grained functional role of each amino acid inside a protein, not just the overall protein function.

hidden.name: Functional resolution
paras: Functional resolution means how well a model understands the internal structure of protein function. A model with high resolution knows not just what the protein does, but exactly which building blocks do each part of the job. A model with low resolution might guess the overall function correctly but fail when asked about specific amino acids.

VenusX measures functional resolution by testing predictions on six types of amino acid labels: which ones are active sites, which bind other molecules, which are evolutionarily unchanged, which form repeating patterns, which form functional chunks, and which are antibody targets. The paper tracks how much accuracy drops when the protein comes from a different evolutionary family than the training set, which is the clearest signal that a model lacks true internal understanding.

heat.caption: Darker means higher accuracy. Models stay dark on in-family proteins (training set) but fade on out-of-family (true test of understanding).

reads.html: Does the model really know which amino acids do each job, or does it just memorize patterns from proteins it saw during training?

The paper measures this by tracking per-residue accuracy (whether the model correctly identifies the role of each amino acid) and plots how much it drops when the protein family is unseen during training.

mechanism.h2: Why this benchmark reveals the real gaps
paras: Whole-protein prediction is too coarse. A model can predict that a protein is an enzyme even if it misses half the amino acids that make the reaction happen. It is like identifying a car as a sedan by looking at the shape, without checking if the engine runs.

VenusX forces models to predict the exact role of each amino acid (residue-level and fragment-level tasks), which requires genuine internal understanding. When a model sees a protein from a different evolutionary family, it cannot lean on surface similarity anymore. The model has to transfer its understanding of how active sites work, how binding sites look, how motifs are organized, and how domains fold. The accuracy drop on out-of-distribution families is the truth test: it shows whether the model learned real mechanisms or just memorized training patterns.

The six task types are not arbitrary. Each one probes a different kind of knowledge: active sites test chemical understanding, binding sites test how other molecules attach, conserved sites test evolutionary knowledge, motifs test pattern recognition, domains test structural chunks, and epitopes test antibody targeting. Together they form a complete picture of whether a model has internalized how proteins actually function at the amino acid level.

stages.s: Protein sequence plus structure (or alignment history)
Model learns which amino acids do each of six jobs
Tested on same protein family (easy test)
Tested on new protein family (hard test, shows real understanding)
Accuracy drop reveals which models actually learned internal structure

math.words: For each amino acid, compute the classification accuracy separately for in-distribution (same evolutionary family) and out-of-distribution (new family). Calculate the drop as the difference. Average across all amino acids and all six task types.
symbols: the model's success rate predicting amino acid roles in proteins from the training family
the model's success rate predicting amino acid roles in proteins from a new, unseen family
how much accuracy the model loses when facing new protein families

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Protein language model on in-distribution (same family): identifies 89 out of 100 amino acids correctly = 89% accuracy.
Same model on out-of-distribution (new family): identifies 71 out of 100 amino acids correctly = 71% accuracy.
Generalization gap: 89% - 71% = 18 percentage points. The model loses nearly a fifth of its accuracy on truly new proteins.
If the gap is small (5%), the model learned general principles; if large (20%+), it memorized the training family.

math.note: A small gap means the model understood the deep structure of proteins; a large gap means it learned surface patterns.

charts.title: Old way: whole-protein benchmark
charts.note: Models look good because whole-protein prediction is easy to fake with surface patterns. Nobody knew the model was failing at the details.

charts.title: VenusX: fine-grained benchmark
charts.note: Different models now show their true strengths and weaknesses. Hybrid models (sequence plus structure) generalize better to new protein families than language-only models, because they rely on physics-based three-dimensional structure that transfers across families, not language patterns unique to one family's evolutionary history.

items.html: A model can achieve 90% accuracy on proteins from the same evolutionary family simply by learning surface patterns specific to that family. It will crash on new families.
If the 878 thousand labels from the databases contain mistakes, no model can score perfectly. VenusX depends on data quality from InterPro, BioLiP, and SAbDab.
Real proteins may have other functional features VenusX does not test, such as allosteric sites (places where binding elsewhere changes behavior) or cross-protein interaction surfaces.

Compare models on the hardest splits (cross-family generalization) and weight the six task types equally if you want a fair overall score. Report both in-distribution and out-of-distribution numbers always.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small protein classifier using one of the baseline models (e.g., a pretrained protein language model). Train it on 5 thousand samples from one protein family (e.g., kinases). Then evaluate it on 1 thousand new samples from the same family and 1 thousand samples from a completely different family (e.g., antibodies). Plot the accuracy separately for each group. The demo makes it impossible to miss: the model's performance collapses on the new family, because the model learned to recognize patterns in kinase sequences that do not appear in antibody sequences, so when asked to label antibody amino acids, it has no learned mapping to fall back on.
demo.metric_eq: Out-of-distribution drop = (accuracy on same family) - (accuracy on new family)
demo.closing: If the drop is large (15% or more), the model learned only family-specific patterns and does not truly understand protein mechanics at the amino acid level.
